I / Navigation Architecture

The student's map of their own learning — progress visible at every level

The student sidebar is architected around the lifecycle of a learning interaction: you review what you need to study (Home), you work through it (Study Queue, Practice, Exams), you understand what went wrong (Results), you see your long-term progress (Mastery, USMLE Readiness), and you track your history (History). Every nav item serves a different time horizon — from today's queue to semester-long Step 1 readiness.

M1–M4 phased experience

M1 — Year 1
Foundation

Study Queue is primary. Practice unlocked. No exams yet (first semester). USMLE Readiness shows Basic Science coverage. Mastery starts building from lecture concepts. Streak and daily queue are the main engagement loops.

M2 — Year 2
Integration

All 8 tabs active. Formal exams deployed. USMLE Step 1 readiness tracker becomes prominent. Why Wrong? explanations begin forming mental models. BKT data is rich enough to show real decay patterns.

M3 — Clerkship
Clinical application

Practice mode emphasizes Bloom 4-6 (clinical reasoning). Step 2 readiness tracker activates. Self-test mode prominent for shelf exam prep. Mastery view shows clinical consequence ordering — highest-stakes gaps first.

M4 — Advanced
Readiness

USMLE Step 2 CK coverage tracking dominates. Historical analytics show 4-year mastery arc. Practice mode allows NBME simulation (timed, full-length). Residency application readiness estimate from coverage data.

II / Student Onboarding

From enrollment to first study session — 5 steps, under 8 minutes

Student onboarding is the opposite of faculty onboarding. Faculty create content; students consume it. The student onboarding goal is: (1) set their USMLE target date so the readiness tracker is calibrated, (2) connect them to their enrolled courses so their queue populates immediately, (3) give them a first taste of the study queue before they can leave. The product should feel like it already knows what they need to study on day one.

1
Account creation — MSM SSO or magic link
MSM email verified via SAML SSO (preferred) or magic link. No password creation — reduces friction. First name, last name, graduating year (M1/M2/M3/M4), and student ID. The graduating year determines which USMLE readiness tracker activates (Step 1 for M1-M2, Step 2 for M3-M4) and which phase of content is shown first.
2
Confirm enrolled courses — auto-populated from SIS integration
If SIS (Student Information System) integration is configured, enrolled courses appear automatically. Student confirms: "Is this your current schedule?" One tap to confirm. If SIS isn't integrated: manual course code entry (e.g., MEDI-601). Joining a course immediately gives access to faculty-approved assessment items for that course. The course connection is what populates the study queue and practice bank.
3
Set USMLE target date — calibrates the readiness tracker
Calendar picker for expected Step 1 and/or Step 2 exam date. System immediately shows: "Based on your target date, you have 14 months to cover 987 Step 1 topics. At your current course load, your expected coverage by exam day is 68%." This creates urgency and context for the coverage gap view. The target date can be updated at any time in settings.
4
Set daily study goal — drives streak and queue scheduling
Three presets: Focused (15 min/day — 5 cards), Balanced (30 min/day — 12 cards), Intensive (45 min/day — 20 cards). Custom option for specific card count. This setting directly controls the BKT queue depth shown daily. Students can change it at any time. The system also learns from actual completion rates over the first two weeks and may suggest adjusting the goal up or down.
5
Do your first 3 cards — immediate engagement before leaving onboarding
Three pre-selected cards from the first week of their enrolled course. Short, confidence-appropriate (Bloom 1-2). The goal is to get a successful first session: answer 3 questions, see the feedback, see the mastery bar move. Completion shows: "3 questions answered · 2 correct · First study streak started." This guarantees every student has a non-zero streak from day one. Onboarding completes and lands them on the full Home dashboard.
III / Home Dashboard

The daily briefing — what to study, what's coming, where you stand

The student home is not a dashboard in the enterprise sense. It's a morning briefing. The primary question it answers: "What should I do right now?" The secondary question: "Am I on track?" Everything else — exams, streaks, mastery — is context that supports those two questions. The layout is intentionally mobile-first because students study on their phones.

IV / Study Queue

BKT-driven spaced retrieval — the right concept at the right time

The BKT mastery model

Bayesian Knowledge Tracing models each concept as a hidden state: either the student "knows" it or "doesn't know" it. After each response, the model updates: a correct answer raises p_mastery, an incorrect answer lowers it, and both correct and incorrect answers are discounted for guessing and slipping probabilities. Critically, even correctly-answered concepts decay over time following a modified Pimsleur curve — concepts answered correctly 3+ times still re-appear, just less frequently. The study queue is the BKT scheduler's output: these are the specific concepts that need review today to maintain mastery above the p_mastery ≥ 0.95 threshold.

BKT scheduling algorithm — parameters

ParameterValueMeaning
p_init0.10Prior probability of knowing a concept before any exposure
p_transit0.20Probability of learning a concept from a wrong answer
p_slip0.10Probability of answering incorrectly despite knowing (slip)
p_guess0.20Probability of answering correctly without knowing (guess)
Mastery threshold0.95p_mastery ≥ 0.95 = "mastered" (concept exits daily queue)
Decay modelPimsleur-modified exponentialEven mastered concepts decay — requeue interval: 1d → 3d → 7d → 14d → 30d
Queue depthBased on daily goal settingBalanced=12, Focused=5, Intensive=20 (adjustable in settings)
Clinical orderingHigh-consequence firstWithin same p_mastery tier, topics with high clinical consequence (fatality risk) appear before low-consequence topics
V / Practice Mode

IRT-powered free practice — student-configured, algorithmically selected

IRT item selection

Practice mode uses 3-parameter logistic Item Response Theory (3PL-IRT) to select items that match the student's current estimated ability (theta). The system maintains a running theta estimate per USMLE system domain based on all historical responses. Practice items are selected from the pool where difficulty parameter (b) ≈ theta ± 0.5, avoiding questions that are too easy (boring) or too hard (demoralizing). As the session progresses and the student answers correctly or incorrectly, theta updates in real time and the next item is selected accordingly. This is adaptive testing at the practice level — each session is automatically calibrated to challenge the student appropriately.

VI / Exam Delivery

Timed, scrambled, auto-saved — the full exam experience

C01 — Exam auto-save is a production requirement

Every answer selection is auto-saved immediately to session_answers in Supabase. If a student loses connectivity, closes the browser, or their device crashes mid-exam, every answer they selected persists. When they re-open the exam, they see exactly the state they left. There is no "submit" behavior where in-progress answers can be lost. The final submission converts session_answers into an immutable exam_attempts record via an atomic Postgres RPC call.

Exam scrambling — per-student item and option order (C02)

Each student receives items in a unique randomized order derived from their student_id + exam_id + item_order_seed. Within each item, the A-E options are also shuffled per student using a separate option_shuffle_seed. This prevents answer sharing between students taking the same exam simultaneously. The scrambling is deterministic — if a student loses connectivity and re-enters the exam, they see the same order they started with. Faculty see the canonical item format when reviewing; scrambling is transparent to the faculty view.

VII / Results + Why Wrong?

The most important moment in learning — understanding what you missed and why

Why Wrong? — the AI explanation system

Most assessment tools tell you what the right answer was. Why Wrong? tells you why your reasoning was wrong — specifically, which misconception you most likely held that caused you to choose the incorrect option. This is powered by the misconception graph in the knowledge graph: each wrong answer option is connected to one or more misconception categories (via Toulmin warrant-claim chains), and after submission, Haiku generates a personalized explanation that names the misconception, explains why it's wrong, and gives the correct mental model. This is the difference between assessment and learning.

Wrong answers — Why Wrong? explanations
Q7 — Incorrect
Pharmacology Bloom 3
A patient with HFrEF (EF 25%) develops significant bradycardia after starting carvedilol. The attending decides to switch to a more cardioselective beta-blocker. Which agent would be the most appropriate replacement?
B. Atenolol Your answer
C. Metoprolol succinate Correct answer
Why Wrong? — AI explanation

You chose atenolol, which is indeed highly cardioselective (β1 > β2). The reasoning was likely: "cardioselective → atenolol." However, this misses a critical distinction for heart failure: atenolol has no evidence of mortality benefit in HFrEF. The three beta-blockers proven to reduce mortality in HFrEF are carvedilol (non-selective), metoprolol succinate (β1-selective), and bisoprolol (β1-selective). Atenolol is used in hypertension and stable angina but is not approved for HFrEF management. The misconception here is conflating "cardioselective" with "evidence-based for HFrEF" — these are different properties. Next time: for HFrEF, ask "which beta-blocker has RCT mortality data?" not just "which is most cardioselective?"

Q9 — Incorrect (flagged)
Cardiovascular Bloom 4
A 58-year-old man with HFpEF (EF 60%) presents with dyspnea on exertion. His BNP is 340 pg/mL. Which of the following best explains why ACE inhibitors have NOT demonstrated the same mortality benefit in HFpEF as in HFrEF?
A. Afterload reduction is not beneficial in preserved EF Your answer
D. The pathophysiology of HFpEF is heterogeneous and less dependent on neurohormonal activation Correct
Why Wrong? — AI explanation

Your answer reflects a partially correct but incomplete mental model. Afterload reduction is indeed beneficial in HFpEF — it reduces pulmonary congestion and improves exercise tolerance. The actual reason ACE inhibitors lack mortality evidence in HFpEF is more fundamental: HFpEF is not a single disease but a heterogeneous syndrome driven by multiple mechanisms (inflammation, fibrosis, microvascular dysfunction, metabolic syndrome effects). Unlike HFrEF where RAAS overactivation is a dominant pathophysiologic driver, HFpEF doesn't have one central mechanism to target. Large trials (CHARM-Preserved, I-PRESERVE) failed to show benefit precisely because the patient population was mechanistically diverse. The clinical lesson: absence of evidence ≠ evidence of harm; in HFpEF, current treatment focuses on symptom management and comorbidity treatment.

Clinical consequence ordering

When multiple concepts are at the same mastery level, the queue prioritizes by clinical consequence — the real-world severity of getting this concept wrong. Concepts in the "immediately life-threatening" tier appear in the queue before concepts in the "benign/supportive" tier, even if p_mastery is identical.

TierDescriptionExample conceptsQueue priority modifier
Tier 1Immediately life-threatening if missedSTEMI recognition, PE treatment, sepsis protocols+3 priority points
Tier 2Significant morbidity if missedHFrEF GDMT, medication dosing, contraindications+2 priority points
Tier 3Important but manageable if missedClassification systems, grading scales+1 priority point
Tier 4Diagnostic/supportive knowledgeEponym authors, historical contextNo modifier
IX / USMLE Readiness Tracker

Step 1 and Step 2 coverage — built from actual question responses, not self-report

Coverage is earned, not assigned

The USMLE readiness tracker does not show coverage based on which lectures a student attended or which courses they're enrolled in. Coverage is earned only through answering questions — for each USMLE topic, coverage is granted when a student has answered at least one question that maps to that topic. This distinction matters: a student can sit through a Heart Failure lecture without actually knowing anything about Heart Failure. The tracker shows what they've demonstrated via responses, not what they've been exposed to. This is a fundamentally more honest readiness measure than lecture attendance tracking.
